column1: Gap Summary — Normative Coverage by Requirement

column5: RFC 6749, RFC 9068 and RFC 8693 cover the protocol roles and the representation of subject and actor; chains of actors, runtime identity metadata and identifier scoping are only partially covered. Normative gaps: ephemeral agent or sub-agent identity, and the distinction between upstream and downstream delegation participants.

RFC 8693 distinguishes delegation from impersonation and, with RFC 9068, represents the actor separately from the subject; identity collapse across hops is only partially addressed (nested act is informational). Normative gap: preserving accountability across multiple hops, including rejection of a truncated or modified actor history.
RFC 9396 + RFC 8707 provide strong structured/resource constraint coverage; tool-invocation, workflow-scoping, and authority monotonicity enforcement are normative gaps.

RFC 6749, RFC 6750, RFC 7662 and RFC 9396 assign validation to the AS and the RS; rejection of unknown constraint types is defined for the AS only. Normative gaps: designation of an enforcement actor per delegation constraint, and enforcement responsibilities across heterogeneous agent platforms.

RFC 6749, RFC 8414, RFC 9728, RFC 8693, RFC 9068 and RFC 9635 cover the protocol roles, their discovery, the subject/actor distinction and the client instance. Normative gaps: the delegator role, the delegate agent role, downstream delegation participants and delegation ancestry semantics.

RFC 9068 (expiration) and RFC 7662 (active state) cover the lifetime of a single token; RFC 7009 covers revocation as an early end of validity only in part. Normative gaps: a downstream token's lifetime bounded by its upstream token's remaining validity, the upstream/downstream lifetime relationship across multi-hop chains, and renewal and reauthorization of persistent delegation chains.

RFC 7009, RFC 7662 and RFC 6750 cover single-token revocation, revocation-state discovery and rejection; revocation latency and the freshness/availability declaration are only partially covered. Normative gaps: cascading revocation, subtree revocation, partial (per-permission) revocation, and revocation during in-progress execution.
RFC 9068 + RFC 9449 + RFC 8705 cover JWT/PoP validation; delegation ancestry validation, depth validation, and multi-hop provenance validation are normative gaps.

RFC 6750 + RFC 9700 + RFC 9449 + RFC 8705 cover bearer/PoP artifact security (possession, presentation, replay); transfer and forwarding, storage and disclosure, derivation, and audience and context restrictions are only partially covered; the consequences of artifact compromise, including chains across trust domains, are a normative gap.

RFC 9449 (DPoP) and RFC 8705 (mTLS) cover sender-constrained token binding; RFC 7800 covers PoP key semantics. Remaining gaps: runtime/workload-context binding — no RFC binds delegated authority to a specific executing workload or agent instance — and rotation and failure behavior for binding credentials.

RFC 6749, RFC 8693 and RFC 9396 allow narrower scope and authorization details in a derived token, and GNAP admits multi-RO grants, without mandating or verifying attenuation. Normative gaps: a formal attenuation algebra, a monotonic attenuation guarantee across hops, and a verifiable proof that downstream authority is bounded by upstream authority. Biscuit and ZCAP-LD illustrate what is needed.

RFC 8693 enables token transformation and represents actor chains only informationally. Normative gaps: explicit permission to re-delegate, explicit prohibition of re-delegation, delegation depth limits, and inheritance rules for the authority of a re-delegated token.

Gap: delegation provenance beyond the per-token metadata and informative act chain — execution provenance, invocation provenance (orchestration requests), tool invocation provenance, human approval provenance and disclosure semantics — has no normative coverage (5 of 7 sub-requirements).

Gap for execution-time human oversight, R13(b)–(i): no RFC defines approval checkpoints, denial or override semantics, oversight policies, action classification, approval binding, validity window, approver unavailability or approval-request volume control. Only R13(a), authorization-time interaction (RFC 6749 §4.1, RFC 9635 §2), is covered.

RFC 6750 + RFC 7662 + RFC 8693 cover bearer/token-state/exchange errors; delegation ancestry failure, depth violation, unauthorized re-delegation, and human-approval failure semantics are normative gaps.
